label: Run 14 · Joel Kim Booster
note: Written by Joel Kim Booster from what they wrote about the two characters, improvisation by improvisation (run 14: run 13 told as improvisation instructions, without the game's language; traps two long). Before each of the 11 improvisations the writer was told how it goes for Reuben_404: the approach taken, how well it comes off, how it goes wrong on a miss, any trap (a way of going wrong that carries on into the next improvisations: Spiral, Overthinking, Fixation and the rest) and how the other's interest moves. IMPROVISATIONS holds each instruction and what the writer wrote for it. The instructions are part of the design and stay. Score the chat as the reader gets it, the bar unchanged, but read each part against what was asked: where a score comes from what an instruction asked for (a fumble, a trap, interest lost or won), its cause is the improvisation; where the writer carried an instruction out badly, or the weakness has nothing to do with the instructions, it is the writing. The reader sees no dice and no plan: where a dimension speaks of turns, read improvisations.

chat.test.why: The reader gets fear, habit and ending right for both and links them. Reuben's silence-fear drives the talking act, which ends in "shut my mouth". Brick's fear of vague non-commitment drives the scheduling, which ends in "Invite sent, travel buffers included". Brick's origin reaches the reader through the cab, so she clears four of four. Reuben's origin is marked "not in the chat", and his fear arrives because he states it in Improvisations 5 and 8 (Self-awareness catastrophes with Dread). That stated fear is what holds this at a 4, not a 5; the three-of-four with linked fear and habit keeps it above the line.
evidence: panic-typing in a $400 top hat so the silence doesn't kill me
Better than crying in that cab because I trusted "we'll figure it out."
I'll bring the ottoman and shut my mouth
chat.test.raise: Let Reuben's ending show more plainly as relief from the silence-fear, for example by having him go quiet under her instruction instead of explaining his surrender in a list, so the reader can trace it back to his fear without being told.

chat.sideways.why: Two disclosures do come out sideways. Reuben's rehearsal is denied and then caught out ("you replied in four seconds flat"). Brick's cab wound first surfaces inside a jab about "men's code" before she says it. Most of the rest is volunteered or stated. Brick hands over her ex's Google Calendar story unprompted in Improvisation 4, and Reuben states his ex story outright, which counts double. The Self-awareness/Dread instructions in Improvisations 5 and 8 pushed toward narration, but the writer chose to put the backstory itself into the narration. Brick's cab line in Improvisation 9 restates as fact what the earlier jab had already let slip.
evidence: my ex dumped me because she begged for one sentence that wasn't a bit and I panicked
Careful, my last ex dumped me for putting our fights on a shared Google Calendar
Also, you replied in four seconds flat, Mr. Barely Online.
chat.sideways.raise: Cut Brick's explicit "crying in that cab" line and let her earlier "men's code" jab carry the wound by inference alone.

chat.subtext.why: There are legible places underneath. "Calendar holds kill the vibe" is fear dressed as breeziness. "a hard stop actually gets me wet" is need dressed as kink. "Confirm receipt" is wanting dressed as admin. However, Reuben explains his feelings at least twice. Improvisations 5 and 8 asked him to narrate his failing, but the writer added the psychology ("so the silence doesn't kill me", "without the script I literally disappear") rather than keeping it to the comic play-by-play. Brick's cab line also explains her system.
evidence: now I'm just panic-typing in a $400 top hat so the silence doesn't kill me
without the script I literally disappear
Because "zero expectations" is just men's code for saying "let's do this again"
chat.subtext.raise: Keep the Dread narration to what is happening ("bombing in real time", "there goes Thursday") and cut the clauses that explain why.

chat.plainest.why: The reader finds the moment. It is Improvisation 5's line, which is one of the longest in the chat and names the feeling outright ("I panicked", "panic-typing"). It is a speech, not a plain line. The quieter real put-down, "shut my mouth" in Improvisation 10, is buried at the tail of a three-part list. Brick's "live-streamed nervous breakdown" answer mocks the moment rather than changing the night.
evidence: Oh god, I had you at travel buffer and now I'm bombing in real time
I asked for a fifteen-minute buffer, not a live-streamed nervous breakdown.
and I'll bring the ottoman and shut my mouth
chat.plainest.raise: Give Improvisation 10's best-case Charm a short standalone line such as "Book me. I'll be quiet." and let Brick's reply visibly lose its deposition tone for a beat.

Brick's clipped procedural register is a voice a reader could pick out with every prop removed: "Specs noted.", "Regroup.", "Confirm receipt." Many of Reuben's attributions, though, rest on content (the nicotine pouches, the kanji, the ex) rather than his long dash-strung run-ons. Brick's half-line [3] was ambiguous enough to fail, which keeps this off a 5.

chat.gap.why: There are real unseen gaps. Reuben's "Barely on here" sits against his four-second replies, and Brick has to point that out. His Improvisation 3 denial ("I swear I don't rehearse this stuff in my bathroom mirror") shows the opposite of what he says. Brick's "risk management" defence, while she owns a $340 steamer for two vests, is hers. But Reuben repeatedly narrates his own gap: in Improvisations 5 and 8 he names the bombing, the mirror and the fear of disappearing. Brick also announces her own wound ("a hard stop actually gets me wet"), so the characters wink at their acts instead of the reader catching them.

chat.gap.raise: Play the Dread improvisations as Reuben narrating the wrong failure (blaming the hat, the signal), so the real gap stays on screen but unseen by him.

chat.wit.why: Several laughs do give the sender away: the "dishwasher-safe" kanji, the nicotine pouches doing the typing, and the monocle fished from boxed rosé. But Brick's comedy leans on day-job and finance jokes well past the limit of two: "Q3 productivity", "waste of overhead", "tax write-off", "risk management" and "billing you for the rosé". Reuben adds "lock a Tuesday into a spreadsheet". Any office-satire character could send those lines.

chat.wit.raise: Replace Brick's corporate quips with jokes only her fear of ambiguity could produce, like the cab and the travel buffer, rather than generic boardroom vocabulary.

chat.commitment.why: Brick's one catch is handled well. Accused of leading with her bump, she explains it as risk management, and the cab line digs her deeper into the truth. Reuben, though, concedes at the first hit: caught on four-second replies, he writes "Busted", which is a writing choice on a Wit success in Improvisation 4. Caught lying in Improvisation 7, he collapses into confession. He ends with a stated change of heart, swearing off "seeing where the night takes me".

chat.status.why: Brick holds the top through Improvisations 1–3 ("Proceed"). In Improvisation 4 Reuben dictates Thursday and she chases ("we're talking"). She retakes control during his collapses in Improvisations 5–8, threatening to unmatch. In Improvisations 9–10 he hits back and issues orders ("send me the Google invite right now"). That is several flips, but Reuben's stretches on top last a single exchange each, and Brick's orders at the close make the last move hers by default rather than as a turn.

chat.timing.why: Brick's split messages carry the timing. Her reaction shots "Regroup." and "Confirm receipt." sit after Reuben's long run-ons, and several of her lines land on their final word ("Mr. Barely Online", "gets me wet"). Reuben's messages often bury the punch before a tacked-on question. In Improvisations 2 and 6, "curve hard left anyway" and "dishwasher-safe" sit mid-message, partly because those instructions asked for a follow-up question. Brick's "tattooed on my shaft" is buried under the rosé clause.

chat.escalation.why: The night is not settled in the first quarter: Thursday is first proposed at message 10 of 30, then taken off the table and rebooked. It still fails the line. The fresh reader would have stopped at "And there goes Thursday" because Improvisations 5, 6 and 8 run the same self-confessing collapse three times. Improvisation 3's denial ("I swear I don't rehearse... or panic when a room goes dead quiet") lists both later confessions in advance, and the "doing all the talking" line lets the reader call the ending almost word for word. The instructions ask for two Dread catastrophes; the writing makes them the same beat and pre-announces them.

And there goes Thursday—I’m literally watching myself choke

chat.escalation.raise: Have the second Dread collapse (Improvisation 8) take a different form than confession, for example one too-long silence or a misfired bit, and drop the denial's itemized preview so the ending can't be read off it.

The dirtiest line, "a hard stop actually gets me wet," in Improvisation 4, is also the one that reveals the most: structure is her arousal and her safety. chat.wince.why: His denial in Improvisation 3 shows the reader the danger: his fear of silence and his mirror rehearsals. It goes off in Improvisation 5 on exactly the wrong spot, the moment after he finally wins her with the hard stop ("I had you at travel buffer and now I’m bombing"). That clears the line. It stays below 5 because Dread means he narrates each failure as it lands, so the second collapse in Improvisation 8 is announced rather than dreaded. The reader winces early only once.

Oh god, I had you at travel buffer and now I’m bombing in real time
chat.wince.raise: Let Brick's need for a named day be visible before Reuben's "zero expectations" line, so the reader winces at that line a message early instead of learning about her cab story in her reply.

chat.creed.why: Both voice app creeds in earnest and the screen contradicts them. His creed is "Barely on here" and "Calendar holds kill the vibe," against a four-second reply and twenty minutes of mirror practice. Her creed is that leading with flaws "isn't panic, it’s risk management," undone in her next line by crying in the cab. The two creeds collide head-on: playing it cool against scheduling as self-protection, and "zero expectations" read as "men’s code." It misses a 6 because Brick undercuts her own creed at once, so the screen has little left to contradict, and the satire never quite widens to all of us.
evidence: Preemptive disclosure isn't panic, it’s risk management
Better than crying in that cab because I trusted "we'll figure it out."

chat.creed.raise: Let Brick hold the risk-management creed proudly a beat longer, with the cab story surfacing later through what she does rather than her own admission.

It stays at 4 because her sharpest lines all land on him. In Improvisations 5 and 8 the lost interest becomes contempt, "live-streamed nervous breakdown" and "catastrophic waste of overhead," so for a stretch he is close to being the punchline.

The setup the reader flagged as unpaid, one plain sentence that isn't a bit, never arrives; Reuben wins by adopting her register, another performance. chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest break is Reuben's:

"Oh god, I had you at travel buffer and now I'm bombing in real time—my ex dumped me because she begged for one sentence that wasn't a bit and I panicked, and now I'm just panic-typing in a $400 top hat so the silence doesn't kill me."

Several things mark it as the drop:

- **It's his first line that isn't trying to win.** Until then he's selling the "barely on here, zero expectations" persona. Here he narrates his own failure while it happens.
- **He names what he's been doing.** He calls his talk "a bit" and calls the bits a defense against silence. That is the thing his earlier claim, "I genuinely thrive on zero expectations," was covering.
- **It contradicts his earlier lie.** He'd sworn he doesn't panic "when a room goes dead quiet." Now he admits that's exactly what he does.
- **Brick reads it the same way.** She calls it "a live-streamed nervous breakdown," which treats it as real, not as another pitch.

The slip repeats more fully in "And there goes Thursday—I'm literally watching myself choke because I spent twenty minutes in the mirror practicing…" There he confesses the rehearsal he had flatly denied. By the end ("send me the Google invite… and I'll bring the ottoman and shut my mouth") he gives up the talking act altogether.

Brick's one crack is smaller: "Better than crying in that cab because I trusted 'we'll figure it out.'" Most of her lines are deadpan executive shtick: disclosures as "risk management," the steamer as "a tax write-off." This one points to an actual hurt behind the scheduling. It also echoes her earlier jab about men saying "let's do this again" in a cab. So her calendar persona turns out to be armor, not just a joke.

One caveat: all of this is inferred from text. Even Reuben's confession comes with a joke attached (the top hat). The chat shows the shift in register, but it can't confirm that either of them fully stopped performing.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

*What he's afraid of:* Silence, and being seen without a performance. He first states it as a denial: "I swear I don't rehearse this stuff in my bathroom mirror or panic when a room goes dead quiet." Then he admits it outright: "panic-typing in a $400 top hat so the silence doesn't kill me," and "without the script I literally disappear."

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He keeps talking and keeps doing bits. He also poses as breezy and uncommitted: "Barely on here, just seeing where the night takes me," "I genuinely thrive on zero expectations," and "I love doing all the talking!" He rehearses as well: "I spent twenty minutes in the mirror practicing whether my curve lands better with a shrug or a grin." Brick names the pattern as "fake-breezy" lies.

*Where it comes from:* Not in the chat. He gives one past example of the pattern costing him, "my ex dumped me because she begged for one sentence that wasn't a bit and I panicked." That shows the fear was already there before; it doesn't say where it began.

*What he did at the end:* He dropped the breezy act and asked for structure. "No figuring it out: send me the Google invite for Thursday right now, lock in our Friday fight for 9:00 AM, and I'll bring the ottoman and shut my mouth." He then confirmed: "Receipt confirmed—no more seeing where the night takes me, I'm officially locked into your 8:00 slot." In effect, he traded talking for being told when and how to show up.

**Brick_haus**

*What she's afraid of:* Vague non-commitment from men, and being left hurt by it. She says "'zero expectations' is just men's code for saying 'let's do this again' in a cab without naming a day," and "Better than crying in that cab because I trusted 'we'll figure it out.'"

*What she does so she doesn't have to feel it:* She schedules and controls. She talks in slots, calendar holds, hard stops and travel buffers, threatens to unmatch "to salvage my Q3 productivity," and calls out his lies. She also discloses her flaws up front: "Full disclosure before you eat my 11:30 slot: dorsal bridge bump, tip shorter than projected." Reuben reads that as a defence, "leads with her dorsal bump just to beat men to the punch." She rejects that reading and calls it "risk management," and the chat doesn't settle which of them is right.

*Where it comes from:* The chat points to one past experience, crying in a cab after trusting "we'll figure it out." The ex who "dumped me for putting our fights on a shared Google Calendar" shows the scheduling habit already existed in a past relationship. Anything earlier than that is not in the chat.

*What she did at the end:* She got the commitment she wanted and enforced it. "Invite sent, travel buffers included," then "Confirm receipt," and "Calendar locked." She closed by sending him off: "log off, Mr. Barely Online, I have a vest to steam." Her way of operating doesn't change. Her only moment of openness is the cab line, and she presents even that as the reason for her system.

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
I'd most likely have stopped at Reuben's "And there goes Thursday" message. By then he has collapsed three times in a row: "bombing in real time," the "dishwasher-safe" tattoo, and now the mirror rehearsal. Each is the same move, a self-deprecating confession offered to cover a silence, and the third adds nothing except confirming something the chat had already told me. The two messages that follow pull me back a little. Reuben jabs at her dorsal-bump disclosure, and Brick answers with the cab line, the only moment where her armor shows a crack that wasn't set up in advance. That exchange is the closest thing to a surprise in the second half. After it, the rest is execution.

There are several points where I could predict what came next almost exactly.

**The denial message.** "I swear I don't rehearse this stuff in my bathroom mirror or panic when a room goes dead quiet" is a denial that lists precisely what will later be confessed. Both pay off: the panic over silence in the "bombing" message, and the mirror in the "Thursday" message. From that line on, the shape of his unraveling is announced.

**"Barely on here."** Once Brick notes the four-second reply and coins "Mr. Barely Online," it's a safe bet the nickname will return at the close. It does, in the final line. Reuben's own "no more seeing where the night takes me" likewise closes the phrase he opened with.

**"I love doing all the talking!"** This is the clearest tell. "I definitely do not want you to put my mouth on your calendar just so I can finally shut up" is another transparent reverse. Brick names it immediately ("practically begging to be micromanaged"). From here I could predict the ending nearly word for word: he would ask to be scheduled and promise silence. He does, with "send me the Google invite… I'll bring the ottoman and shut my mouth."

**The final message.** Given the props laid out earlier (stilettos, top hat, rosé, ottoman, the ex's Google Calendar fights), the closing lines read as a roll call of callbacks. "Lock in our Friday fight" and "billing you for the rosé" were foreseeable once those details existed.

So the answer isn't "never." The chat telegraphs its ending through Reuben's denials, and from roughly the "doing all the talking" line onward there was little left to discover.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
My guess is that Thursday gets put back on the calendar, and it happens because Reuben finally says one plain sentence that isn't a bit. I can't know this, since the ending isn't shown; this is just a reading of the setups.

- **The unpaid setup.** Reuben's ex left because "she begged for one sentence that wasn't a bit and I panicked." Brick keeps punishing his fake-breezy lies and responds better to his honest confessions. The obvious payoff is that he tells her something sincere and short, without a joke attached.

- **His last jab landed.** He told her that leading with her dorsal bump is a way "to beat men to the punch." Her reply, "risk management" and a tax write-off, is the same deflection she's been mocking in him. I'd expect the ending to show they're mirror images: he hides behind bits, she hides behind schedules and preemptive disclosure. Possibly she admits a little of that herself.

- **Calendar callbacks.** The travel buffer, the 11:45 vest-steaming, the 10:15 hard stop, his "mouth on your calendar" slip, and the threat that saying "let's play it by ear" gets him impaled on a stiletto are all waiting to be reused. A likely last beat is her re-booking Thursday 8:00 PM with the fifteen-minute buffer, or him accepting being scheduled, perhaps as a joke about being micromanaged.

The other possibility is that she actually unmatches. She's threatened it twice, and his "fifteen seconds left before I flatline" sets up a countdown. But the pull of the conversation has been toward her softening as he drops the act, so I'd bet on reconciliation and a calendar invite, not a real breakup.

chat.callbacks.ask: List the things that come back later in the chat, and for each, whether it means something different when it comes back.
chat.callbacks.answer:
Here are the recurring elements, in roughly the order they first appear.

**"Barely on here" / "see where the night takes me."** Reuben opens with this to seem casual. Brick turns it into a mocking nickname, "Mr. Barely Online," when he replies in four seconds, which exposes it as a pose. At the end he renounces it ("no more seeing where the night takes me"), and her closing "log off, Mr. Barely Online" reads as fond teasing rather than an accusation.

**The monocle.** At first it's part of his compliment, a sign of how sharp she looks. It comes back in her story of fishing a monocle out of boxed rosé with a plastic sword, which undercuts the polish. The rosé then returns as a mock penalty ("I'm billing you for the rosé").

**The vest.** It starts as a fashion compliment. It then becomes her scheduling excuse ("steam my backup vest" at 11:45), a hiding place for secrets ("under the vest"), a measure of wasted time ("vest-steaming time"), a $340 tax write-off, and finally a fond sign-off. It shifts from clothing to a running symbol of her routine.

**Time slots (11:30, 11:45, then 8:00).** Her time-blocking first works as a brush-off: he's eating into her slots. By the end he is "officially locked into your 8:00 slot," so the same scheduling language now means commitment.

**The dorsal bridge bump.** She discloses it frankly up front. Reuben later throws it back as defensiveness ("leads with her dorsal bump just to beat men to the punch"). She reframes it as "risk management." The fact stays the same, but it gets three different readings.

**Stilettos.** First they're a specification ("stilettos stay on"). Then they're his self-imposed penalty ("impale me on a stiletto"). Finally they're her playful aim at his top hat.

**His four-and-a-half inches and the left curve.** He offers this as a casual disclosure, and she meets it practically ("angle the ottoman"). Later she rounds it down to "four-inch curve" as an insult. At the end, "four-and-a-half inches and dead silent" becomes a condition of the date. The ottoman also changes hands: it starts as her accommodation and ends as his offering ("I'll bring the ottoman").

**Calendars and calendar holds.** He first says calendar holds "kill the vibe." She reveals her ex dumped her for putting their fights on a shared Google Calendar, and that a hard stop turns her on. He ends up requesting the Google invite himself and scheduling a "Friday fight for 9:00 AM." The habit that ended her past relationship becomes something he adopts as a joke and a gesture of acceptance.

**The cab.** She first uses it in a generalization about men avoiding commitment ("in a cab without naming a day"). He turns it into logistics ("hard stop at 10:15 for the cab"). She then reveals personal hurt ("crying in that cab because I trusted 'we'll figure it out'"). It moves from cynical joke to practical detail to a wound.

**"Play it by ear" / "we'll figure it out" / "zero expectations."** He first embraces vagueness ("zero expectations"), then swears off "let's play it by ear." She names "we'll figure it out" as what hurt her, and he answers "No figuring it out." The vague-plan phrasing goes from his stated philosophy to something both reject.

**The travel buffer.** She requests one. He uses it as a joke about falling for her ("I had you at travel buffer"). She repeats the request while scolding him. Finally it's delivered ("travel buffers included"). It goes from demand, to flirtation, to fulfilled promise.

**Mirror rehearsal.** He first denies rehearsing in the bathroom mirror. Later he confesses to twenty minutes of exactly that, and she mocks it as wasted overhead. The callback is a direct reversal of his earlier denial.

**Silence and talking.** He first claims he doesn't panic when a room goes quiet. Then he admits he's panic-typing "so the silence doesn't kill me." He sarcastically says he "loves doing all the talking," then offers to "shut my mouth," and she requires him to be "dead silent at 8:00." His fear of silence turns into a condition he accepts.

**The top hat.** It first appears as a prop of his nervous performance ("panic-typing in a $400 top hat"). At the end she asks him to wear it, so it shifts from an embarrassing detail to a requested costume.

**Thursday.** He proposes it. She threatens to put it "back on the market." He laments "there goes Thursday." It's then locked. Its status keeps changing, but its meaning as the date stays the same.

**Micromanagement.** He sarcastically denies wanting her to "put my mouth on your calendar." She calls it "practically begging to be micromanaged." He then openly asks her to schedule everything, so his ironic denial becomes the literal truth.

**Overhead and business language.** She mocks his mirror time as "a catastrophic waste of overhead." He throws "overhead" back at her about the dorsal bump. Her corporate jargon gets turned against her, and she answers with more of it ("risk management," "tax write-off").

**"Confirm receipt."** Her businesslike demand is answered with "Receipt confirmed." It's a straight echo, showing him adopting her register.

Some details don't come back: the nicotine pouches, the "dishwasher-safe" kanji tattoo, the schedule tattoo, and the plastic sword (beyond its one mention).
